title: Quality Control: Levey–Jennings Charts, Westgard Rules and QC Failure
summary: Read a Levey–Jennings chart, apply 1₂s (warning), 1₃s and 2₂s (rejection) rules, match the multirule set to the sigma metric, and follow CLIA requirements for control frequency and corrective action after QC failure.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 11 Hits 2, 6 and 8 (first lesson for Ch. 11). Checked against Peng 2022, Ramachandra 2025, Teshome 2021 and 42 CFR 493.1256, 493.1267 and 493.1282 (eCFR, current as of 2026-10-01). US rules only. Not taught: “1₂s as rejection gives ~10% false alerts” (Hit 2) and the reviewer’s exact failure sequence “new vial → recalibrate” (Hit 8, taught only as the general corrective-action workflow); CLSI C24 target-setting (Hit 4) and power-function figures (Hit 5) — not in the sources read.

objectives: Read a Levey–Jennings chart and apply 1₂s, 1₃s and 2₂s rules.
Relate the sigma metric to the choice of QC rules and number of controls.
Apply CLIA control frequency and corrective action after QC failure.

scenes.title: One point outside 2 SD — stop the line?
scenes.altText: An invented Levey–Jennings chart for glucose control level 1 (mean 100 mg/dL, SD 2): days 1–9 scatter around the mean; day 10 = 104.5 (+2.25 SD). A second chart for level 2 shows day 10 at +3.4 SD. Patient results from the morning run are waiting to be released. Question token: “Warning, reject — and what happens to the patients already run?”

cues.text: A glucose control chart: mean 100, standard deviation 2. Today the level 1 control reads 104.5, just over 2 SD above the mean.
On another day, the level 2 control lands beyond 3 SD. Patient results from that run are waiting to be released.
Is each a warning or a rejection, and what happens to the patients already tested?

props.label: Warning or reject? What about patients?

scenes.title: The Levey–Jennings chart
scenes.altText: Chart card (Peng 2022): control results are plotted over time against the mean with ±1, ±2 and ±3 SD lines; the mean and SD are calculated from initial runs (e.g., the first 20 batches). Requirement card (42 CFR 493.1256, US): for each quantitative procedure, run two control materials of different concentrations at least once each day patient specimens are assayed; statistical parameters (mean and SD) must be defined for each batch and lot of control material; control results must meet acceptability criteria BEFORE patient results are reported. Blood gases (42 CFR 493.1267): one control sample each 8 hours of testing, with low and high values each day.

cues.text: A Levey–Jennings chart plots control results day by day against their mean, with lines at 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations. The mean and SD come from an initial series of runs, such as the first 20.
US CLIA rules require, for each quantitative test, two control levels of different concentrations at least once each day patients are tested, with a defined mean and SD for each control lot.
Controls must meet the acceptability criteria before any patient result is reported.
Blood gases are stricter: one control every 8 hours of testing, with low and high levels each day.

scenes.title: Warning and rejection rules
scenes.altText: Rule card (Peng 2022): 1₂s — one control more than 2 SD from the mean = WARNING, not out of control; 1₃s — one control beyond 3 SD = REJECT (random error); 2₂s — two consecutive controls beyond 2 SD on the same side = REJECT (systematic error). Multirule card (Ramachandra 2025; Teshome 2021): multirule procedures such as 1₃s/2₂s/R₄s/4₁s/10x combine rules; rule choice depends on the sigma metric — Sigma = (TEa − |bias|)/CV: ≥ 6σ → 1₃s with N = 2; 5–6σ → 1₃s/2₂s/R₄s; 4–5σ → add 4₁s, N = 4; 3–4σ → all rules including 10x, N = 6. Back to the hook: level 1 at +2.25 SD = 1₂s warning (check other rules); level 2 at +3.4 SD = 1₃s rejection.

cues.text: One control beyond 2 SD, the 1-2s rule, is a warning, not an out-of-control run. It tells you to look harder.
One control beyond 3 SD, the 1-3s rule, rejects the run. Two consecutive controls beyond 2 SD on the same side, the 2-2s rule, also reject it.
Multirule procedures combine rules such as 1-3s, 2-2s, R-4s, 4-1s and 10x. How many you need depends on the method’s sigma metric: allowable error minus bias, divided by imprecision.
A six-sigma method can run on 1-3s alone; a 3 to 4 sigma method needs every rule and more controls.
Back to the chart: plus 2.25 SD is a 1-2s warning. Plus 3.4 SD breaks 1-3s: reject the run.

props.title: 2₂s = REJECT
lines: Two in a row > 2 SD, same side

scenes.title: When QC fails
scenes.altText: Corrective-action card (42 CFR 493.1282): when control or calibration results fail the laboratory’s acceptability criteria, all patient results obtained in the unacceptable run and since the last acceptable run must be evaluated to determine whether they were adversely affected, and corrective action must ensure accurate, reliable results. Combined with 493.1256(f): do not report patient results until QC is acceptable. Workflow (schematic): hold results → investigate cause (control material, reagent, calibration, instrument) → correct → rerun QC → rerun/review affected patients back to the last acceptable run → document. Back to the hook: level 2 at +3.4 SD → hold the morning results, fix, re-run QC, and re-evaluate patients back to the last good run.

cues.text: When controls fail, the rules are clear. Do not report patient results until the controls are acceptable.
Every patient result in the failed run, and since the last acceptable run, must be evaluated to see whether it was affected.
In practice: hold results, find the cause, such as the control material, reagent, calibration or instrument, correct it, and rerun the controls.
Then rerun or review the affected patient samples, and document everything.
Back to the hook: with level 2 beyond 3 SD, hold the morning results, fix the problem, and re-evaluate patients back to the last good run.

props.title: QC failed (42 CFR 493.1282)
lines: Evaluate patients since last good run

props.label: Hook: hold, fix, re-run QC, recheck patients to last good run

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Any point beyond 2 SD rejects the run” (✓ 1₂s is a warning; 1₃s and 2₂s reject); “Fix the QC, then release the waiting results” (✓ evaluate all patient results since the last acceptable run); “One control level a day is enough” (✓ CLIA: two levels of different concentrations each testing day for quantitative tests).

cues.text: Trap one: any point beyond 2 SD rejects the run. No: 1-2s is a warning. Rejection comes from rules such as 1-3s or 2-2s.
Trap two: once QC is fixed, release the waiting results. No: every patient result since the last acceptable run must be evaluated first.
Trap three: one control level a day is enough. US rules require two levels of different concentrations each testing day for quantitative tests.

props.title: ✗ “Fix QC, then release.”
lines: ✓ Re-evaluate patients since last good run

scenes.title: Two warns, three stops
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Two warns, three stops; two twos in a row also stop.” Tokens: 1₂s = warn · 1₃s = stop · 2₂s = stop · sigma high → fewer rules. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: two warns, three stops, and two twos in a row also stop. A point beyond 2 SD warns; beyond 3 SD stops; two consecutive beyond 2 SD on the same side stops.
Where it breaks: some labs use 1-2s or other rules differently in their QC plan; R-4s, 4-1s and 10x add more stops; and the right rule set depends on the method’s sigma metric and local policy.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Levey–Jennings: mean ± 1/2/3 SD · 1₂s warning · 1₃s and 2₂s reject · rule set by sigma = (TEa − |bias|)/CV”, “CLIA: 2 levels each testing day (blood gas 1 per 8 h) · QC acceptable before reporting · failed QC → evaluate patients since last good run”.

cues.text: On a Levey–Jennings chart, 1₂s is a warning while 1₃s and 2₂s reject the run, and when QC fails no patient result is reported until the cause is corrected and every result since the last acceptable run has been evaluated.

props.label: 2 levels/day (gas 1 per 8 h) · QC OK before reporting · recheck since last good run

explanation.what: Plain language: labs run samples of known value (controls) alongside patients and plot them on a chart; if a control drifts too far from its usual value, the run is held and fixed before patient results go out, and patients already tested are checked again. Scientific terms: internal quality control, Levey–Jennings chart, mean, standard deviation, Westgard rules (1₂s, 1₃s, 2₂s, R₄s, 4₁s, 10x), random vs systematic error, sigma metric, total allowable error (TEa), bias, CV, corrective action.
explanation.why: Controls behave like patient samples in the measuring system, so a control far outside its expected distribution signals an error that could also affect patients. A single point beyond 3 SD suggests random error; repeated points beyond 2 SD on one side suggest systematic shift. Methods with large error margins (high sigma) need fewer rules to detect clinically important error.
explanation.measure: Peng 2022: 1₃s out of control; 1₂s warning; 2₂s (two consecutive warnings) out of control; limits from initial runs (first 20 batches). Ramachandra 2025: Sigma = (TEa − Bias%)/CV%; ≥ 6σ → 1₃s N = 2; 5–6σ → 1₃s/2₂s/R₄s N = 2; 4–5σ → +4₁s N = 4; 3–4σ → all incl. 10x N = 6. 42 CFR 493.1256: two control levels each testing day for quantitative tests; mean/SD defined per lot; QC acceptable before reporting. 493.1267: blood gas one control each 8 h. 493.1282: evaluate patient results since last acceptable run; corrective action.
explanation.differs: Warning (1₂s) vs rejection (1₃s, 2₂s); random error (single extreme point) vs systematic error (consecutive same-side shifts); high-sigma (simple QC) vs low-sigma (multirule, more controls) methods.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: classify a Levey–Jennings pattern, choose warning vs reject, CLIA control frequency, and what to do with patient results after a QC failure.

questions.stem: A glucose control (mean 100 mg/dL, SD 2) reads 107 mg/dL; the other control level is within 1 SD. Which rule is violated?

options.rationale: Correct. 107 is 3.5 SD above the mean, beyond the 3 SD limit.
Incorrect. The value exceeds 3 SD, not just 2 SD.
Incorrect. 2₂s requires two consecutive controls beyond 2 SD on the same side.
Incorrect. A point beyond 3 SD is out of control.

questions.stem: Two consecutive runs show the level 1 control at +2.3 SD and +2.6 SD. What is the interpretation?

options.rationale: Correct. Two consecutive controls beyond 2 SD on the same side reject the run.
Incorrect. Consecutive same-side warnings constitute a 2₂s rejection.
Incorrect. Repeated same-side shifts point to systematic error.

questions.stem: A run fails QC after 30 patient samples were analysed. Under 42 CFR 493.1282, what must be done with those patient results?

options.text: Evaluate all results in the failed run and since the last acceptable run for adverse effect
options.rationale: Correct. Patient results back to the last acceptable run must be evaluated; corrective action must ensure accuracy.

options.text: Release them once the next QC passes
options.rationale: Incorrect. Results must not be reported until QC is acceptable and affected results are evaluated.
Incorrect. Commenting does not satisfy the requirement to evaluate and correct.
Incorrect. Results are evaluated and corrected, not deleted; all control procedures must be documented.

claims.text: Levey–Jennings chart; 1₂s warning; 1₃s and 2₂s rejection; initial-run limits.
Sigma formula and sigma-based rule selection.
CLIA control frequency (2 levels daily; blood gas 8 h); acceptable QC before reporting.
Corrective action and evaluation of patient results since last acceptable run.
1₂s rejection ≈ 10% false alerts; exact failure sequence (new vial, recalibrate); CLSI C24 target setting; power-function probabilities; R₄s/4₁s/10x definitions.
